content.text: Sound is one of the most important and familiar phenomena in our daily lives. From the alarm clock that wakes you up in the morning to the music you listen to, from the conversations you have with friends to the rumble of thunder during a storm, sound is everywhere. But what exactly is sound, and how does it travel from one place to another?

Sound is a longitudinal mechanical wave that is produced by vibrating objects and travels through a medium by means of compressions and rarefactions. Unlike light and other electromagnetic waves, sound cannot travel through a vacuum; it requires a material medium such as air, water, or a solid to propagate. Understanding the physics of sound helps explain everything from how musical instruments work to how medical ultrasound imaging produces images of the inside of the body.

In this lesson, we will explore the nature of sound waves, how they are produced and transmitted, the factors that affect the speed of sound, the relationships between frequency, pitch, amplitude, and loudness, and the many applications of sound in science and technology.

Sound is a longitudinal wave. This means that the particles of the medium through which the sound travels vibrate back and forth in the same direction as the wave is travelling. When a sound source vibrates (such as a loudspeaker cone, a guitar string, or a tuning fork), it pushes the surrounding air molecules forwards and pulls them backwards in rapid succession.
When the source pushes the air molecules forward, they crowd together, creating a region of high pressure called a
. When the source pulls back, it creates a region of low pressure called a
. These compressions and rarefactions propagate outward from the source as a wave, carrying energy through the medium.

It is important to emphasise that the air molecules themselves do not travel from the sound source to your ear. Each molecule oscillates back and forth about its equilibrium position, passing the disturbance along to its neighbours. It is the pattern of compressions and rarefactions (the energy) that travels, not the air itself.

One of the most important properties of sound is that it cannot travel through a vacuum. Sound requires a medium (a substance made of particles) to travel through. This can be demonstrated with the classic bell jar experiment:

An electric bell is placed inside a glass jar (bell jar) connected to a vacuum pump. When the bell is switched on with air in the jar, the sound is clearly audible. As the air is gradually pumped out, the sound gets fainter and fainter. When most of the air has been removed, the bell can be seen vibrating but almost no sound is heard. This demonstrates that sound needs air (or some other medium) to carry it from the source to the listener.

This is fundamentally different from light, which is an electromagnetic wave and can travel through a vacuum. This is why in space, where there is no air, there is silence. Explosions in space would produce no sound, despite what is often depicted in movies.
All sounds are produced by vibrating objects. When an object vibrates, it disturbs the surrounding medium (usually air), creating sound waves. Examples include:
The stretched drum skin vibrates when struck.
The string vibrates when plucked, and the vibration is amplified by the guitar body.
An electromagnetic cone vibrates back and forth, pushing air to create sound waves.
The metal prongs vibrate at a specific frequency when struck.
The vocal cords in the larynx vibrate as air passes over them.
If the vibration stops, the sound stops. You can demonstrate this by striking a tuning fork and then touching it to a surface to stop the vibrations; the sound immediately ceases.

There are several methods to measure the speed of sound:
Method 1: Direct timing over a known distance

Two people stand a known, large distance apart (e.g., 400 m). One person creates a loud sound (such as clapping or banging two boards together) while the other starts a stopwatch when they see the action and stops it when they hear the sound. The speed is calculated using
. This method is not very accurate because human reaction time introduces significant error, but it gives a reasonable estimate.

A person stands a known distance from a large flat wall (at least 50 m away). They clap their hands and measure the time for the echo to return. The sound travels to the wall and back, so the total distance is twice the distance to the wall:
To improve accuracy, the person can time multiple echoes (e.g., clap rhythmically so each clap coincides with the return of the previous echo) and divide the total time by the number of intervals.

Two microphones are placed a known distance apart and connected to an electronic timer. A sharp sound is made near the first microphone. The timer starts when the first microphone detects the sound and stops when the second microphone detects it. This gives a much more accurate measurement of the time interval.
is the number of complete vibrations (compressions and rarefactions) produced per second, measured in hertz (Hz). Frequency is a physical, measurable quantity.
is the perception of how "high" or "low" a sound is. Pitch is a subjective sensation experienced by the listener, but it is directly related to frequency:
A high-frequency sound wave is perceived as a high-pitched sound (like a whistle or a soprano voice).
A low-frequency sound wave is perceived as a low-pitched sound (like a bass drum or a deep male voice).
The lowest note on a piano has a frequency of about 27.5 Hz.
Middle C on a piano has a frequency of about 262 Hz.
The highest note on a piano has a frequency of about 4186 Hz.
A dog whistle can produce frequencies above 20,000 Hz, which are inaudible to humans.

is the maximum displacement of the vibrating particles from their rest position. For a sound wave, a larger amplitude means the compressions are more compressed (higher pressure) and the rarefactions are more rarefied (lower pressure). Amplitude is a physical, measurable quantity.
is the perception of how "loud" or "quiet" a sound is. Loudness is a subjective sensation, but it is directly related to amplitude:
A sound wave with a large amplitude is perceived as loud.
A sound wave with a small amplitude is perceived as quiet.
The energy carried by a sound wave is proportional to the square of the amplitude. Doubling the amplitude quadruples the energy carried by the wave.
Loudness is measured in decibels (dB) on a logarithmic scale:
0 dB: the threshold of hearing (the quietest sound a healthy human ear can detect)
85 dB: heavy traffic (prolonged exposure can cause hearing damage)
100 dB: a power drill or loud music
140 dB: a jet engine at close range (immediate hearing damage)

Sound waves, like all waves, can be reflected. When a sound wave hits a large, hard, flat surface (such as a cliff face, a building wall, or a mountain), it bounces back. This reflected sound is called an

For a distinct echo to be heard, the reflecting surface must be far enough away that the reflected sound arrives at the listener's ear after the original sound has finished. The human ear can distinguish two sounds as separate if they are at least about 0.1 seconds apart. The upper limit of human hearing typically decreases with age. Many adults cannot hear frequencies above 15,000 Hz, and the limit decreases further with continued exposure to loud sounds.

Ultrasound is sound with frequencies above 20,000 Hz, beyond the upper limit of human hearing. Ultrasound waves behave just like ordinary sound waves but their short wavelengths give them useful properties:

Ultrasound waves are directed into the body and reflect off boundaries between different tissues (such as the boundary between muscle and bone, or between fluid and tissue). The reflected echoes are detected and processed by a computer to create an image. Ultrasound imaging is widely used in pregnancy scans to monitor the development of a fetus. It is safe because it does not use ionising radiation.

High-intensity focused ultrasound can be used to break up kidney stones (lithotripsy). The ultrasound waves are focused on the stone, causing it to fragment into pieces small enough to pass naturally out of the body.

Ultrasound is used for non-destructive testing of metal structures, welds, and pipelines. Cracks or voids inside the material reflect ultrasound differently from solid material, allowing defects to be detected without cutting the material open.
Ultrasonic cleaners use high-frequency vibrations in a liquid to dislodge dirt and contaminants from delicate items such as jewellery, electronic components, and surgical instruments.
As mentioned above, sonar systems use ultrasound pulses to measure distances underwater. This is used for navigation, fish detection, and mapping the ocean floor.
Some tape measures and parking sensors use ultrasound to measure distances. A pulse of ultrasound is emitted, and the time for the echo to return is used to calculate the distance.

The human ear can detect sounds from 20 Hz to 20,000 Hz. Calculate the wavelength range of audible sound in air (speed of sound = 340 m/s).

The wavelength range of audible sound is from 1.7 cm to 17 m. This enormous range explains why sound waves interact with objects of many different sizes; low-frequency sounds with long wavelengths can diffract around buildings and corners, while high-frequency sounds with short wavelengths tend to travel in straighter lines and are more easily blocked.

Misconception 1: Sound can travel through a vacuum

Sound is a mechanical wave that requires a medium to travel through. It cannot travel through a vacuum. This is why there is no sound in space. In contrast, light (an electromagnetic wave) can travel through a vacuum.
Misconception 2: Sound travels faster in air than in solids

The opposite is true. Sound travels fastest in solids (where particles are closest and bonds are strongest) and slowest in gases (where particles are far apart). The speed of sound in steel is about 15 times faster than in air.

The speed of sound in a medium is independent of the loudness (amplitude) of the sound. A whisper and a shout travel at the same speed in air. The speed depends on the properties of the medium (temperature, density, elasticity), not on the amplitude of the wave.

Pitch and loudness are independent properties of sound. Pitch is related to frequency, while loudness is related to amplitude. A high-pitched sound can be quiet (a soft whistle), and a low-pitched sound can be loud (a bass drum). The two properties are controlled independently.
Misconception 5: Echoes are only heard from mountains

Echoes occur whenever sound reflects off any large, hard surface. Buildings, walls, cliffs, and even large vehicles can produce echoes. The requirement is that the reflecting surface is at least about 17 m away (so the reflected sound is separated in time from the original) and is large and hard enough to reflect the sound effectively.

Ultrasound at the levels used in medical imaging is considered very safe. Unlike X-rays and gamma rays, ultrasound is non-ionising and does not damage DNA. This is why it is the preferred imaging method for monitoring pregnancies. Very high-intensity ultrasound (such as that used in lithotripsy) does require careful control, but diagnostic ultrasound is not harmful.

Sound consists of compressions (high-pressure regions) and rarefactions (low-pressure regions) that propagate through a medium.
Sound requires a medium to travel; it cannot travel through a vacuum.

Sound travels much faster in solids than in gases. The speed of sound in steel (railway track) is approximately 5000-6000 m/s, compared to about 340 m/s in air. This means sound from the approaching train reaches the listener's ear through the track much sooner than through the air. The particles in a solid are closely packed with strong intermolecular forces, allowing vibrations to be transmitted very quickly from one particle to the next.

Concert halls are designed to control the reflection of sound so that the audience hears clear, high-quality audio. Hard, flat surfaces reflect sound and can produce echoes if the reflected sound reaches listeners more than about 0.1 s after the direct sound. This would make speech or music unclear. Curved walls, angled panels, and soft materials (such as carpets, curtains, and padded seats) are used to absorb sound and reduce unwanted reflections. Some reflections are desirable: a controlled amount of reverberation (where reflected sounds blend together shortly after the direct sound) gives music a rich, full quality. Too much reverberation makes speech hard to understand, while too little makes music sound flat and dry. The shape and materials are chosen to give an optimal reverberation time, typically 1-2 seconds for concert halls.

The lowest audible frequency has a wavelength of 17 m, which is comparable to the size of a large room or building. This explains why low-frequency sounds diffract easily around obstacles and can be heard around corners. The highest audible frequency has a wavelength of only 1.9 cm, comparable to the size of a finger or a small gap. High-frequency sounds therefore travel more in straight lines and are more easily blocked by obstacles, which is why treble sounds are more directional than bass sounds.
